ety.text: Inherited from Middle English wyf, wif, from Old English wīf (“woman, wife”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīb, from Proto-Germanic *wībą (“woman; wife”). Cognates Germanic cognates include Scots wife (“wife; woman”), North Frisian wuf, wüf (“wife, woman”), Saterland Frisian Wieuw (“woman; wife; female”), West Frisian wiif (“wife; woman”), Cimbrian baibe, baip (“wife; woman”), Dutch wijf (“woman; female”), German Weib (“woman; wife; female”), German Low German Wiev (“woman; female”), Mòcheno baib (“woman”), Vilamovian bow (“wife; woman”), Yiddish ווײַב (vayb, “wife; woman”) Danish, Norwegian Bokm…

senses.d: A married woman, especially in relation to her spouse.
The female of a pair of mated animals.
ex: A new wife for the gander is introduced into the pen.
Mentally scarred for life, love is war / And some chicks are just too hard to wife
Mecca knew she wasn't lying. She had the type of beauty that made niggas want to wife her.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French femme, from Old French fame, feme, fenme, femme, from Latin femina; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-éh₂ (“(the one) nursing, breastfeeding”), derivation of the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”).

ety.text: Inherited from Latin mulier (nominative). The alternative forms reflect the Latin accusative mulierem.
Inherited from Old Spanish mugier, from Latin mulierem. Compare Portuguese mulher.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese esposa, from Latin spōnsa.

From Old Galician-Portuguese muller, moller (hence also Galician muller), from Latin mulierem (“woman; wife”), of uncertain origin. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ- (milk; to milk). Cognate with Mirandese mulhier, Spanish mujer, Catalan muller, Italian moglie, and Romanian muiere.
